q: What did Marshall McLuhan's laws of media (the tetrad) actually claim, how have scholars applied, extended or criticised it since Laws of Media appeared in 1988, and has anyone tried to test it empirically?

review.sentence: Enhancement and obsolescence are a pair: what a medium amplifies in the foreground, it pushes out of use somewhere else.
review.why: Tyler shows McLuhan explicitly denied that obsolescence means a medium is pushed out of use: "clearly, newspapers did not die out with the advent of radio", and McLuhan's own example is that handwriting is obsolescent yet far more of it is done than before printing. The section's gloss converts a claim about loss of force into a claim about displacement from use.

review.sentence: On the wording alone, reversal is not a forecast about the future but a claim about a tendency already present in the thing being described; that reading is an inference from the phrasing, not something the McLuhans state.
review.why: This is presented as the section's own inference when the sources record McLuhan stating it: he "always urged that one should 'Never predict anything that hasn't already happened'", and his interest was in what is "inherent" in existing technologies. The section undersells documented support and wrongly says the McLuhans never say it.

sentences.sentence: In the form McLuhan settled on they are: what does the artefact enhance; what does it make obsolete; what does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier; and what does it flip into when pushed to extremes [3].

Library and Archives Canada, which holds the McLuhan papers, presents this as the compressed statement of the position set out in *Laws of Media* (1988), the book Eric McLuhan assembled and published after his father's death [3].
The first is scope: the questions are to be put to "any artefact", not only to communications media [3].

The archival account is explicit that the four laws "exist simultaneously", and that although McLuhan sometimes talked as if they succeeded one another, he did not intend them to be read in chronological order [3].

McLuhan was not claiming that one medium entirely supersedes another — newspapers did not die out with radio — and his own example is that handwriting has been obsolescent since printing while far more of it is done daily now than before printing [8].

Retrieval is explicitly retrospective: the third question asks what the artefact brings back that had been obsolesced earlier, which makes every tetrad a comparison between a new form and an older one [3].
Reversal is the most distinctive and the least checkable: it asks what the artefact becomes at its limit [3].

McLuhan insisted reversal was not futurology, urging that one should never predict anything that hasn't already happened, and Tyler reads the four laws as interrogating what is implicit or inherent within a medium rather than forecasting what follows it [8].
The archival account states that it is "not meant to be a scientific tool", but an instrument for exploring the grammar and syntax of an artefact, a way of describing situations in process [3].

Writing for software testers, Michael Bolton takes McLuhan's definition to cover tools, devices, thoughts, artefacts, technologies and concepts, and describes the laws as four probes, testing heuristics, to which every medium can be submitted [9].
Thomas Hylland Eriksen, applying it to the Internet, valued it for producing "distinctions between different kinds of effects" [2] — a taxonomic use, not a predictive one.
Two competent readers can therefore produce incompatible tetrads for the same artefact, as McLuhan and McLuhan did for wine on a single page of the book [8].

McLuhan first published the four laws in *Technology and Culture* in 1975, and Tom Tyler documents that McLuhan "asserted that they constituted testable hypotheses", and that he presented them as a scientific method modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability, citing the 1975 *Technology and Culture* article and a 1977 piece in *ETC* [8].

In Tyler's account, McLuhan "believed that the tetrad provides" what McLuhan called "an ordering of thought and experience" [8] — an ordering not yet overturned, rather than a statement from which predictions follow. *Laws of Media: The New Science* (1988) pushed the claim further, and it did so in the voice of the co-author.
Eric McLuhan wrote that the four questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [8].

Library and Archives Canada, which holds his papers and mounts the official exhibition on the tetrad, states that the tetrad "is not meant to be a scientific tool", but an exploratory instrument for the grammar and syntax of each artefact [3].

Venable's *Flaws in McLuhan's Laws* appeared in *Technology and Culture* in 1976, with McLuhan's reply in the same issue, and Tyler points readers to that exchange as the place where the case against the laws is argued at length [8].
On a single page of the book, p. 206, they give two different tetrads for wine [8].
The second, on the same page, has it enhancing food and "the occasion", obsolescing inhibition, retrieving "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reversing into "hangover" and insult [8].
Tyler's verdict on the scientific claim is blunt: the idea that these are "scientific laws" in anything like the ordinary sense of the phrase is "preposterous" [8].
What survives is the weaker thing McLuhan said in 1967 — "I don't explain — I explore" — and the weaker thing he said in 1975, that the tetrad orders thought and experience [8].

Thomas Hylland Eriksen used the tetrad in 1996 to organise the effects of the Internet, running it at three separate levels — technological, social and cultural — so that the same four slots produced different content depending on the frame chosen [2].

At the technological level his tetrad has the Internet intensifying nonterritorial information flow, rendering letters and magazines obsolete, retrieving text-based information, and flipping into interactive real-time multimedia [2].
Eriksen was candid about the instrument's quality, calling the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" while judging it worth trying out [2].

Published in *Glocality* in 2016, it takes the tetrad as a framework for examining a new device's effects on individuals and society, filling enhance, obsolesce, retrieve and reverse with smartphone content [1].

Library and Archives Canada's own exhibition demonstrates it by filling in a tetrad for the cell phone, and describes the four laws as tools for analysing the patterns of effects that different technologies produce [3].

Michael Bolton, a software tester writing in *Better Software* in October 2007, presents the four laws as four probes — he calls them "testing heuristics" — to which every medium can be submitted, and cites Federman and de Kerckhove's *McLuhan for Managers* (2003) as the bridge [9].

Logan, who collaborated with McLuhan for six years, re-runs *Understanding Media* chapter by chapter and adds chapters on the smartphone, social media, games, virtual reality and AI, with a section on the laws of the media and the evolution of technology [12].
His publisher describes the book as updating McLuhan to analyse the new media McLuhan foresaw but never lived to examine [12].

Writing in *Game Studies* in 2008, Tyler could name only two precedents for using the tetrad on digital media: Stuart Moulthrop's 1991 discussion of hypertext and David Miles's 1996 application of a single law to *Myst* [8].

Enhancement becomes a claim about computational complexity; obsolescence becomes remediation, drawing on Bolter and Grusin; retrieval becomes the recovery of effortful, "extranoematic" participation from analogue games and sports; reversal becomes pervasive and persistent play rather than immersion [8].

"The Missing Media Laws" appeared in *Explorations in Media Ecology* in 2007 under a title that reads like an attack on the tetrad; it is by Marshall McLuhan and Eric McLuhan, a recovered text, not a critical article [15].

The practitioners say so themselves: the *Glocality* essay concludes that "multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad", since interpretation rests on the analyst's own perceptions [1].
Eriksen's follow-up remark on his own Internet tetrads is blunter — "all the above is questionable" [2].
In the preface to *Laws of Media*, Eric McLuhan called the tetrad the single biggest intellectual discovery not only of his time but of at least the last couple of centuries [4].

Graham Harman opens his own treatment of the tetrad by noting the gap between that devotion and the response: there is an "obvious disjunction between his devotion to the tetrads and the lack of intensity with which others have pursued them" [4].
Tyler records that the laws are modelled in part on Bacon's four idols and Vico's four axioms, citing the book's introduction, pp. 3–11 [8].

His 2009 chapter in *New Waves in Philosophy of Technology* treats the tetrad as a contribution to metaphysics rather than to media studies, and his 2007 article in *Explorations in Media Ecology*, "The Tetrad and Phenomenology", argues the four laws should be read through phenomenology [16].

By re-running *Understanding Media* chapter by chapter and adding chapters on the smartphone, social media, games, virtual reality and AI, Logan extends the framework's reach to media McLuhan never saw, and places a section on the laws of the media inside an account of the evolution of technology [12].

A 2026 article by Barrientos-Báez, Barceló-Sánchez and Caldevilla-Domínguez in the *Revista de la Asociación Española de Investigación de la Comunicación* applies the tetrad systematically to generative AI, and reports that AI externalises cognitive processes such as synthesis and writing, raising efficiency while activating the law of reversal [10].

Its method is explicit: a qualitative approach based on comparative conceptual analysis, reading McLuhan's texts against recent work in neuroscience, algorithmic sociology and computational creativity [10].

The *Glocality* essay claims that although McLuhan developed the tetrad three decades earlier, it is "universal in nature" and therefore still applicable to present and future developments, its value lying in holding four laws together so that past, present and future are seen at once [1].

No peer-reviewed proposal of a fifth law that was subsequently adopted by other scholars was found in the literature searched; the tetrad remains a fourfold in the applied and theoretical work examined [12][10][1].

Tyler sets out to use the tetrad, warns that it risks operating on Procrustean principles — bothersome empirical details hammered or shorn to fit — and then concludes that as a scientific theory it does deform the research it touches [8].
His verdict on the claim to scientific status is that it is preposterous in anything like the ordinary sense of the phrase [8].

Too loose: conceived as a universal scientific method it is far too vague, since a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any artefact, a huge range of things it might augment, obsolesce, retrieve and reverse into, and the laws therefore do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all [8].
Too rigid: like Procrustes' bed it requires us to fill the gaps, so the analyst supplies content for the fourth box whether or not evidence supports it [8].

On p. 206 of *Laws of Media* the McLuhans give one tetrad for wine — enhancing grape juice, obsolescing commonplace flavours, retrieving ritual observance, reversing into cooking vinegar — and then a second on the same page, in which wine enhances food and the occasion, obsolesces inhibition, retrieves festive spontaneity of speech and gesture, and reverses into hangover and insult [8].
Tyler's inference is that if the authors cannot be sure of the consistency of their own results, it is unlikely that the same conclusions will be drawn by anyone, anywhere, at any time [8].
The example is not isolated: further multiple tetrads for the same artefact appear across pp. 195–207 of the book [8].
Library and Archives Canada's exhibition states flatly that the tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but an exploratory device for describing situations in process [3].

Read alongside the book's subtitle, *The New Science*, and Eric McLuhan's promise that the answers can be checked by anyone anywhere at any time [8], the custodians' caveat is a retreat from the 1988 position.
Venable's *Flaws in McLuhan's Laws* appeared in *Technology and Culture* in 1976 with McLuhan's reply in the same issue, and Tyler directs readers there for the case at length [8].
McLuhan sometimes talked about the four laws as succeeding one another, although the intended reading is that they operate simultaneously [3].
Harman, who is sympathetic, records that few of McLuhan's followers pursued the tetrad with any intensity [4].
Eriksen, an early adopter, calls the laws overambitiously phrased and deterministic and judges his own applications questionable [2].
The applied literature concedes unlimited interpretive latitude as a feature rather than a defect [1].
The tetrad, he writes, does violence to its subject matter, and that violence is redeemed only if the resulting investigation is ultimately constructive [8].
The custodial account says the tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool [3].

A 2023 peer-reviewed application to Facebook and Instagram restates the 1988 ambition — laws that anyone, anywhere, at any time would be able to test, prove or refute — and then concedes that the authors insist there are no single or final answers to the four questions [7].
The 2023 social-media tetrad study states its method plainly: a descriptive case study with data gathered by observation and content analysis [7].

The same article describes earlier work — Levinson on radio, Adam on the smartphone — as authors having "tested" the tetrad on different examples, which shows how loosely the word test circulates in this literature: it means applied to a case [7].

McGuire's 2023 *Four Laws of Microsoft Teams* interviewed eight New Brunswick high school educators who taught in the Teams environment during the 2020–21 school year, the first full pandemic school year [13].

Azzano's 2024 soundscape study is similar in kind: a focus group as the primary method, with observational activities, field recordings, documented materials and memoing, analysed for what the tetrad illuminates [14].

A cross-European study of children's media use found electronic games had taken the third position behind television and audio media, but warned its cross-sectional data was unfit to determine causal relationships between media [8].

The Kaiser Family Foundation's research on 8–18 year olds found television dominant at about 3 hours a day against just over an hour of games, total media time unchanged, and heavy users of one medium likely to be heavy users of others, with no displacement effect [8].

Nick Yee's MMORPG data pointed the other way: players averaged 21.0 hours a week gaming and 7.7 hours watching television, against a national average of about 28 hours of television, which Yee read as support for displacement [8].
Tyler's conclusion is that existing studies are collectively uncertain on whether the enhancement of digital play obsolesces television [8].

Tyler's response was not to score the quadrant but to redefine it, treating obsolescence as remediation rather than replacement, drawing on Bolter and Grusin and on McLuhan's own observation that there is far more handwriting now than before print [8].
Bolton's software-testing article calls the four laws four probes, testing heuristics, and notes that what is seen as ground depends on who is observing and on the choices the observer brings [9].

As Hempell put it in 1996, McLuhan proposed the tetrad as an alternative to a model based on causality, organising an artefact as a resonating interval affected by its own attributes and its surrounding environment [11].

Eriksen, applying the tetrad to the Internet and identity politics, produced the reductio: the Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics [2].

report.body:
## TL;DR

The tetrad is four questions to be asked of any artefact at once: what it enhances, what it makes obsolete, what it retrieves that was obsolesced earlier, and what it reverses into when pushed to its limit. McLuhan called the answers laws and invited falsification, then answered critics with analogy, and the book's custodians now call the tetrad an exploratory device rather than a scientific tool. Scholars since 1988 have applied it widely — to the Internet, the smartphone, games, organisations and generative AI — but the extensions widen its reach without adding any way for it to fail. No empirical test of the tetrad was found. The nearest thing, Tyler's check of the obsolescence quadrant against media-displacement data, came back split between studies and was resolved by redefining the term. It is very likely the tetrad will remain useful as a probe and unlikely it will become a testable theory, because it was built as an alternative to causal modelling.

## Key Findings

- The four laws are questions, not statements, and they are meant to be asked simultaneously of "any artefact" rather than only of communications media [3].
- The fourfold's completeness is inherited rather than derived: the laws are modelled in part on Bacon's four idols and Vico's four axioms [8].
- McLuhan presented the laws as testable hypotheses and a scientific method modelled on Popper, and Eric McLuhan claimed the answers could be checked by anyone, anywhere, at any time [8].
- The McLuhans failed their own reproducibility test: two different tetrads for wine on p. 206 of *Laws of Media*, and further multiple tetrads across pp. 195–207 [8].
- The institutional account now states that the tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool but an instrument for exploring an artefact's grammar and syntax [3].
- Tyler's critique is a double bind rather than a charge of vagueness: the tetrad is too loose to be falsified and too rigid in requiring all four slots to be filled [8].
- Applications since 1988 are extensive and include Eriksen on the Internet [2], a smartphone tetrad in *Glocality* [1], Bolton's software-testing heuristics [9], Logan's *Understanding New Media* [12], and a 2026 application to generative AI [10].
- Harman's extension is the strongest defence: he reads the tetrad through metaphysics and phenomenology, which defends it by shifting its subject from media effects to ontology [4][16].
- No study was found that tests the tetrad as a hypothesis; existing work is descriptive case studies, interview and focus-group studies that use the tetrad as a frame, or professional heuristics [7][13][14][9].
- The closest thing to a test is Tyler's review of the displacement literature on whether games obsolesce television: a cross-European study unfit for causal inference, Kaiser Family Foundation data showing no displacement, and Nick Yee's MMORPG data showing the opposite [8].
- The tetrad was proposed as an alternative to causal modelling, which is why there is no causal prediction to test and why a real test would have to supply the mechanism the framework disclaims [11].
- Applied users state plainly that results depend on the analyst: "multiple interpretations are possible" [1], and the same artefact yields different tetrads for different observers [9].

## Details

### 1. What the four laws actually claim: the four questions, their structure, and their stated scope

The tetrad is four questions, and the wording carries the argument. In the form McLuhan settled on they are: what does the artefact enhance; what does it make obsolete; what does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier; and what does it flip into when pushed to extremes [3]. Library and Archives Canada, which holds the McLuhan papers, presents this as the compressed statement of the position set out in *Laws of Media* (1988), the book Eric McLuhan assembled and published after his father's death [3].

Two features of the wording do most of the theoretical work. The first is scope: the questions are to be put to "any artefact", not only to communications media [3]. The second is simultaneity. The archival account is explicit that the four laws "exist simultaneously", and that although McLuhan sometimes talked as if they succeeded one another, he did not intend them to be read in chronological order [3]. The tetrad is therefore not a sequence of stages — invention, displacement, revival, collapse — but one situation described from four sides at once.

The four questions are not four independent claims. Enhancement and obsolescence are a pair, but obsolescence does not mean elimination. McLuhan was not claiming that one medium entirely supersedes another — newspapers did not die out with radio — and his own example is that handwriting has been obsolescent since printing while far more of it is done daily now than before printing [8]. Obsolescence is loss of force, not disappearance. Retrieval is explicitly retrospective: the third question asks what the artefact brings back that had been obsolesced earlier, which makes every tetrad a comparison between a new form and an older one [3]. Reversal is the most distinctive and the least checkable: it asks what the artefact becomes at its limit [3]. McLuhan insisted reversal was not futurology, urging that one should never predict anything that hasn't already happened, and Tyler reads the four laws as interrogating what is implicit or inherent within a medium rather than forecasting what follows it [8].

The tetrad also carries an instruction about its own use. The archival account states that it is "not meant to be a scientific tool", but an instrument for exploring the grammar and syntax of an artefact, a way of describing situations in process [3]. That sentence sits awkwardly beside the 1988 subtitle, *The New Science*, and the awkwardness is the subject of section 2.

The scope of "medium" is far wider than the word suggests, and the width is what makes the tetrad portable. Writing for software testers, Michael Bolton takes McLuhan's definition to cover tools, devices, thoughts, artefacts, technologies and concepts, and describes the laws as four probes, testing heuristics, to which every medium can be submitted [9]. A procedure that applies equally to a hammer, a poem, a tax form and a language is either a powerful instrument or an empty one, and nothing in the four questions settles which.

What the tetrad does not contain matters as much as what it does. It specifies no unit of analysis, no level at which the answers should be pitched, and no rule for deciding when an answer is right. Thomas Hylland Eriksen, applying it to the Internet, valued it for producing "distinctions between different kinds of effects" [2] — a taxonomic use, not a predictive one. The published applications fill the gap in whatever way the analyst chooses. Two competent readers can therefore produce incompatible tetrads for the same artefact, as McLuhan and McLuhan did for wine on a single page of the book [8]. The absence of a rule is not an oversight in the design; it is the design.

### 2. What the McLuhans meant by "law": the testability claim of 1975–1988 and how they answered their critics

The claim to law was made before the book. McLuhan first published the four laws in *Technology and Culture* in 1975, and Tom Tyler documents that McLuhan "asserted that they constituted testable hypotheses", and that he presented them as a scientific method modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability, citing the 1975 *Technology and Culture* article and a 1977 piece in *ETC* [8]. The framing was deliberately Popperian: a law earns the name by surviving attempts to disprove it. McLuhan's own justification was more modest than the word "law" suggests. In Tyler's account, McLuhan "believed that the tetrad provides" what McLuhan called "an ordering of thought and experience" [8] — an ordering not yet overturned, rather than a statement from which predictions follow.

*Laws of Media: The New Science* (1988) pushed the claim further, and it did so in the voice of the co-author. Eric McLuhan wrote that the four questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [8]. Three commitments sit inside that sentence: universality (any artefact), independence of the analyst (anyone), and reproducibility (the answers can be checked). A testable law needs the second and third. The first makes the theory unfalsifiable by definition, since an artefact that yielded no answers to the four questions would not count as an artefact.

The 1988 book also carries a counter-claim, and it comes from McLuhan's institutional custodians. Library and Archives Canada, which holds his papers and mounts the official exhibition on the tetrad, states that the tetrad "is not meant to be a scientific tool", but an exploratory instrument for the grammar and syntax of each artefact [3]. That page cites *Laws of Media* p. 116, and its reading is the one most scholars now work with: it concedes the falsifiability case while denying that it matters.

The first sustained critique came quickly. W. H. Venable's *Flaws in McLuhan's Laws* appeared in *Technology and Culture* in 1976, with McLuhan's reply in the same issue, and Tyler points readers to that exchange as the place where the case against the laws is argued at length [8]. It matters because it is the one occasion on which the testability claim was contested on its own terms rather than dismissed as a matter of prose style.

The McLuhans then failed their own reproducibility test inside the book. On a single page of the book, p. 206, they give two different tetrads for wine [8]. The first has wine enhancing grape juice, obsolescing commonplace flavours, retrieving ritual observance and reversing into cooking vinegar. The second, on the same page, has it enhancing food and "the occasion", obsolescing inhibition, retrieving "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reversing into "hangover" and insult [8]. If the authors cannot reproduce their own result, the promise that anyone anywhere will reach the same conclusions is not met.

Tyler's verdict on the scientific claim is blunt: the idea that these are "scientific laws" in anything like the ordinary sense of the phrase is "preposterous" [8]. What survives is the weaker thing McLuhan said in 1967 — "I don't explain — I explore" — and the weaker thing he said in 1975, that the tetrad orders thought and experience [8]. The honest summary of what "law" meant is that McLuhan wanted the prestige of Popperian science, used the vocabulary of falsification to invite attack, and answered the attack with analogy.

### 3. Applications since 1988: tetrad wheels, digital media, games, and the tetrad as a working instrument

The first sustained application came quickly and from anthropology rather than media studies. Thomas Hylland Eriksen used the tetrad in 1996 to organise the effects of the Internet, running it at three separate levels — technological, social and cultural — so that the same four slots produced different content depending on the frame chosen [2]. At the technological level his tetrad has the Internet intensifying nonterritorial information flow, rendering letters and magazines obsolete, retrieving text-based information, and flipping into interactive real-time multimedia [2]. Eriksen was candid about the instrument's quality, calling the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" while judging it worth trying out [2].

The dominant post-1988 use is the four-box checklist, and its canonical form is a student essay on the smartphone. Published in *Glocality* in 2016, it takes the tetrad as a framework for examining a new device's effects on individuals and society, filling enhance, obsolesce, retrieve and reverse with smartphone content [1]. The genre is not confined to journals. Library and Archives Canada's own exhibition demonstrates it by filling in a tetrad for the cell phone, and describes the four laws as tools for analysing the patterns of effects that different technologies produce [3].

The tetrad also travelled into professions with no stake in media theory. Michael Bolton, a software tester writing in *Better Software* in October 2007, presents the four laws as four probes — he calls them "testing heuristics" — to which every medium can be submitted, and cites Federman and de Kerckhove's *McLuhan for Managers* (2003) as the bridge [9]. A procedure that a tester runs on a new software feature and a manager runs on a reorganisation is being used as a checklist for anticipating side effects, not as a theory of media.

The most sustained extension inside the tradition is Robert K. Logan's *Understanding New Media* (2010; second edition 2016). Logan, who collaborated with McLuhan for six years, re-runs *Understanding Media* chapter by chapter and adds chapters on the smartphone, social media, games, virtual reality and AI, with a section on the laws of the media and the evolution of technology [12]. His publisher describes the book as updating McLuhan to analyse the new media McLuhan foresaw but never lived to examine [12]. This is the tetrad used as an organising spine for a whole book, which is a more demanding test of the instrument than a four-row table.

Applied work in game studies is thin enough to count. Writing in *Game Studies* in 2008, Tyler could name only two precedents for using the tetrad on digital media: Stuart Moulthrop's 1991 discussion of hypertext and David Miles's 1996 application of a single law to *Myst* [8]. Tyler's own article is the fullest demonstration in the field, and it is instructive because it does not read as a tetrad exercise. Enhancement becomes a claim about computational complexity; obsolescence becomes remediation, drawing on Bolter and Grusin; retrieval becomes the recovery of effortful, "extranoematic" participation from analogue games and sports; reversal becomes pervasive and persistent play rather than immersion [8]. Each quadrant is argued against named research and aimed at a named misconception.

One bibliographic trap is worth recording, because it is easy to mistake for a critique. "The Missing Media Laws" appeared in *Explorations in Media Ecology* in 2007 under a title that reads like an attack on the tetrad; it is by Marshall McLuhan and Eric McLuhan, a recovered text, not a critical article [15].

The pattern across all of these is consistent. The tetrad is used to structure an inquiry, to generate a table, to organise a book or to prompt a professional to look for side effects. It is not used to produce a claim that could fail. The practitioners say so themselves: the *Glocality* essay concludes that "multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad", since interpretation rests on the analyst's own perceptions [1]. Eriksen's follow-up remark on his own Internet tetrads is blunter — "all the above is questionable" [2]. That is not a complaint about the instrument. It is how the instrument is understood by the people who use it.

### 4. Extensions and reformulations: Harman's fourfold test, the search for a fifth law, and tetrads for AI and design

The extensions begin from an enormous claim. In the preface to *Laws of Media*, Eric McLuhan called the tetrad the single biggest intellectual discovery not only of his time but of at least the last couple of centuries [4]. Graham Harman opens his own treatment of the tetrad by noting the gap between that devotion and the response: there is an "obvious disjunction between his devotion to the tetrads and the lack of intensity with which others have pursued them" [4]. Extension since 1988 has therefore taken two forms — more applications, and attempts to supply the metaphysics the McLuhans left out.

The first reformulation is about where the four boxes come from. Tyler records that the laws are modelled in part on Bacon's four idols and Vico's four axioms, citing the book's introduction, pp. 3–11 [8]. That matters for any extension: the fourfold's claim to be exhaustive is inherited from earlier fourfold schemes, not derived from evidence about media. Anyone extending the tetrad to a new technology inherits the completeness claim along with the four questions.

Harman's is the most philosophically ambitious extension. His 2009 chapter in *New Waves in Philosophy of Technology* treats the tetrad as a contribution to metaphysics rather than to media studies, and his 2007 article in *Explorations in Media Ecology*, "The Tetrad and Phenomenology", argues the four laws should be read through phenomenology [16]. The move reframes the tetrad's ambition: if the four laws describe the structure of any object's appearing rather than the effects of any technology, then the failure to produce testable media predictions is beside the point. Harman's reading is the strongest available defence of the tetrad, and it defends it by changing the subject from media effects to ontology.

Logan's *Understanding New Media* is the main extension in McLuhan's own idiom. By re-running *Understanding Media* chapter by chapter and adding chapters on the smartphone, social media, games, virtual reality and AI, Logan extends the framework's reach to media McLuhan never saw, and places a section on the laws of the media inside an account of the evolution of technology [12]. The extension is additive rather than revisionary: the four questions stay as they are, and new artefacts are added to the list they can be asked about.

The most recent extension is to generative AI. A 2026 article by Barrientos-Báez, Barceló-Sánchez and Caldevilla-Domínguez in the *Revista de la Asociación Española de Investigación de la Comunicación* applies the tetrad systematically to generative AI, and reports that AI externalises cognitive processes such as synthesis and writing, raising efficiency while activating the law of reversal [10]. Its method is explicit: a qualitative approach based on comparative conceptual analysis, reading McLuhan's texts against recent work in neuroscience, algorithmic sociology and computational creativity [10]. This is a reformulation in the sense that matters for the report's question — the tetrad extended to a technology that did not exist when the four laws were written, using a method that cannot test them.

Extension in applied hands has taken a different route, and it is a reformulation by assertion. The *Glocality* essay claims that although McLuhan developed the tetrad three decades earlier, it is "universal in nature" and therefore still applicable to present and future developments, its value lying in holding four laws together so that past, present and future are seen at once [1]. That is a claim about the tetrad's scope made without argument, and it is the ordinary way the framework is carried forward.

One extension that is often claimed for the tetrad is not documented in what could be read here. No peer-reviewed proposal of a fifth law that was subsequently adopted by other scholars was found in the literature searched; the tetrad remains a fourfold in the applied and theoretical work examined [12][10][1]. The absence is a finding about the search, not a proof that no such proposal exists, and it is recorded under Open questions.

What unites the extensions is that none of them adds a falsification condition. Harman deepens the metaphysics, Logan widens the corpus, the AI article adds a new artefact, and the applied literature asserts universality. All four make the tetrad apply to more things. None makes it possible for the tetrad to be wrong about any of them.

### 5. The criticism: unfalsifiable or Procrustean, and the strongest dissent from inside and outside media ecology

The sharpest criticism is Tom Tyler's, and its distinguishing feature is that it is not a dismissal. Tyler sets out to use the tetrad, warns that it risks operating on Procrustean principles — bothersome empirical details hammered or shorn to fit — and then concludes that as a scientific theory it does deform the research it touches [8]. His verdict on the claim to scientific status is that it is preposterous in anything like the ordinary sense of the phrase [8]. The same article insists the tetrad has its uses.

The core objection is a double bind, and it is worth stating precisely because it is usually reported as a single charge of vagueness. Tyler argues the tetrad is too loose and too rigid at once. Too loose: conceived as a universal scientific method it is far too vague, since a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any artefact, a huge range of things it might augment, obsolesce, retrieve and reverse into, and the laws therefore do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all [8]. Too rigid: like Procrustes' bed it requires us to fill the gaps, so the analyst supplies content for the fourth box whether or not evidence supports it [8]. The creative mind is thus both the engine of the tetrad's value and the reason it cannot be science.

The wine example is the empirical demonstration of the looseness. On p. 206 of *Laws of Media* the McLuhans give one tetrad for wine — enhancing grape juice, obsolescing commonplace flavours, retrieving ritual observance, reversing into cooking vinegar — and then a second on the same page, in which wine enhances food and the occasion, obsolesces inhibition, retrieves festive spontaneity of speech and gesture, and reverses into hangover and insult [8]. Tyler's inference is that if the authors cannot be sure of the consistency of their own results, it is unlikely that the same conclusions will be drawn by anyone, anywhere, at any time [8]. The example is not isolated: further multiple tetrads for the same artefact appear across pp. 195–207 of the book [8].

The institutional defence concedes the point and denies its importance. Library and Archives Canada's exhibition states flatly that the tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but an exploratory device for describing situations in process [3]. Read alongside the book's subtitle, *The New Science*, and Eric McLuhan's promise that the answers can be checked by anyone anywhere at any time [8], the custodians' caveat is a retreat from the 1988 position. A framework cannot claim testability in its preface and disclaim it in its archive.

The earliest sustained critique came from outside media studies and on logical grounds. W. H. Venable's *Flaws in McLuhan's Laws* appeared in *Technology and Culture* in 1976 with McLuhan's reply in the same issue, and Tyler directs readers there for the case at length [8]. That exchange is where the laws were contested as propositions rather than as prose.

There is also an internal inconsistency about time. McLuhan sometimes talked about the four laws as succeeding one another, although the intended reading is that they operate simultaneously [3]. A framework whose author describes it both as a simultaneous structure and as a sequence has not fixed its own basic ontology, and critics use the slippage.

The dissent from inside the tradition is quieter and, for the tetrad's standing, more damaging. Harman, who is sympathetic, records that few of McLuhan's followers pursued the tetrad with any intensity [4]. Eriksen, an early adopter, calls the laws overambitiously phrased and deterministic and judges his own applications questionable [2]. The applied literature concedes unlimited interpretive latitude as a feature rather than a defect [1]. None of these writers concludes that the tetrad is worthless. All of them treat it as something other than a theory.

Tyler's rescue is the most useful formulation of what survives. The tetrad, he writes, does violence to its subject matter, and that violence is redeemed only if the resulting investigation is ultimately constructive [8]. On that test the tetrad is judged by what it helps a researcher notice, not by whether its claims hold. That is a coherent standard, and it is a different standard from the one the 1988 book set for itself.

### 6. Has anyone tested it empirically? Attempts, results, and what a real test would require

No study was found that tests the tetrad as a hypothesis. That is the direct answer, and the evidence for it is both the absence of such work in the literature searched and the positive statements of the people closest to the framework. The custodial account says the tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool [3]. A 2023 peer-reviewed application to Facebook and Instagram restates the 1988 ambition — laws that anyone, anywhere, at any time would be able to test, prove or refute — and then concedes that the authors insist there are no single or final answers to the four questions [7]. A framework whose own authors deny final answers has no pass/fail condition to test.

What exists instead falls into four kinds, and each is worth separating.

The first is the descriptive case study. The 2023 social-media tetrad study states its method plainly: a descriptive case study with data gathered by observation and content analysis [7]. There is data, but no hypothesis and no measurement of the tetrad's accuracy. The same article describes earlier work — Levinson on radio, Adam on the smartphone — as authors having "tested" the tetrad on different examples, which shows how loosely the word test circulates in this literature: it means applied to a case [7].

The second is the interview or focus-group study that uses the tetrad as its frame. McGuire's 2023 *Four Laws of Microsoft Teams* interviewed eight New Brunswick high school educators who taught in the Teams environment during the 2020–21 school year, the first full pandemic school year [13]. That is real primary data about a real medium. But the tetrad organises the inquiry; nothing in the design could show a quadrant to be wrong. Azzano's 2024 soundscape study is similar in kind: a focus group as the primary method, with observational activities, field recordings, documented materials and memoing, analysed for what the tetrad illuminates [14]. These are the closest things to empirical tetrad work found, and neither is a test.

The third is the closest anyone came, and it is Tyler's own review of the obsolescence quadrant against the displacement literature. This is not framed as a test of the tetrad, but it functions as one. A cross-European study of children's media use found electronic games had taken the third position behind television and audio media, but warned its cross-sectional data was unfit to determine causal relationships between media [8]. The Kaiser Family Foundation's research on 8–18 year olds found television dominant at about 3 hours a day against just over an hour of games, total media time unchanged, and heavy users of one medium likely to be heavy users of others, with no displacement effect [8]. Nick Yee's MMORPG data pointed the other way: players averaged 21.0 hours a week gaming and 7.7 hours watching television, against a national average of about 28 hours of television, which Yee read as support for displacement [8]. Tyler's conclusion is that existing studies are collectively uncertain on whether the enhancement of digital play obsolesces television [8].

That result is the most informative thing in the literature, and it is worth being precise about what it shows. The obsolescence quadrant, applied to one medium pair, generated a claim specific enough to check against audience data — and the data came back split, with a plausible reading on each side. Tyler's response was not to score the quadrant but to redefine it, treating obsolescence as remediation rather than replacement, drawing on Bolter and Grusin and on McLuhan's own observation that there is far more handwriting now than before print [8]. Redefining a term when the evidence cuts against it is exactly the move Tyler identified as Procrustean in the McLuhans. It is also, on his own account, what the instrument is for.

The fourth kind is the professional heuristic. Bolton's software-testing article calls the four laws four probes, testing heuristics, and notes that what is seen as ground depends on who is observing and on the choices the observer brings [9]. That is an explicit statement that the same artefact yields different tetrads for different analysts, which rules out the inter-coder reliability check any test would need.

A real test is not hard to specify, and the specification shows why none exists. It would need an artefact, four quadrants filled independently by several analysts before any outcome is known, a stated observable that follows if a quadrant is right, and a scoring rule. The tetrad supplies none of these, and the reason is structural rather than accidental. As Hempell put it in 1996, McLuhan proposed the tetrad as an alternative to a model based on causality, organising an artefact as a resonating interval affected by its own attributes and its surrounding environment [11]. A framework built as a replacement for causal modelling has no causal prediction to test. Any empirical test would first have to add the causal mechanism the tetrad was designed to avoid.

The unfalsifiability is also visible in the framework's own rhetoric. Eriksen, applying the tetrad to the Internet and identity politics, produced the reductio: the Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics [2]. Four slots filled with the same answer cannot be refuted by any observation. Eriksen printed it, which suggests he saw the problem.

Two things follow, and they are inference rather than finding. First, the tetrad has been applied far more than it has been examined; the applied literature is large and the testing literature is empty. Second, the absence is not a scandal of neglected duty. The framework was built to do something other than predict, and the scholars who use it mostly know that. What is missing is anyone who takes the 1988 subtitle at its word and tries to build the science it promised.


## Beyond this question

Anyone building on the tetrad inherits a specific design constraint from this history. The framework's value is in forcing four kinds of attention at once — amplification, loss of force, retrospective retrieval, and tendency at the limit — and its weakness is that a fluent analyst or a language model can fill all four boxes for any object. Tyler's conditions, drawn from his own applied tetrad, are the practical answer: anchor each quadrant in cited research, report where the evidence cuts against the quadrant, define obsolescence as remediation rather than replacement, keep reversal to what has already happened, and aim each quadrant at a named misconception [8]. Generating rival tetrads for the same artefact and publishing the disagreement turns the wine problem from a defect into a method, since the McLuhans' own practice was to produce several [8].

The most defensible use is the one Harman and Tyler converge on from opposite directions: a counterfactual instrument for surfacing what a technology quietly forecloses. Neither treats it as predictive, and the empirical record gives no basis for treating it as predictive. Anyone who wants a testable claim about a medium's effects should take the claim out of the tetrad and state it separately, as Tyler did with the displacement question, where real studies existed to disagree with each other [8].

## Open questions

No empirical test of the tetrad was found, and the search was not exhaustive. What would settle the question is a study that fills the four quadrants independently, blind to outcomes, with a pre-stated observable and a scoring rule; no such study appeared in any literature searched. The nearest analogue, Tyler's displacement review, tested a claim the tetrad generated rather than the tetrad itself [8].

Inter-coder reliability has not been measured. The applied literature states that interpretations vary with the analyst [1][9], but no study was found that had several analysts code the same artefact and reported agreement. That is the cheapest possible test of the framework's checkability claim, and it appears not to have been run.

The fate of the "fifth law" is unresolved here. The record reports that Eric McLuhan wrote that his father spent the rest of his life looking for a fifth law and for a single case where one of the four did not apply, without success, but that claim was not traced to a primary source in this pass. No peer-reviewed proposal of a fifth law adopted by other scholars was found.

Several sources were read only in part or through secondary report. The Venable–McLuhan exchange of 1976 is known through Tyler's citation and not read in full [8]. Levinson's "tetrad wheels" and the 1978 tetrad conference are reported secondhand and could not be verified against a primary text. Harman's 2009 chapter was read in part and his 2007 article only at the level of its bibliographic record [16]. The 2026 AI article was read from its abstract and method statement rather than its full argument [10]. *Laws of Media* itself is access-restricted at the Internet Archive and was not read directly; all quotations from it in this report come through Tyler's article, which is why the page references are his.

The independence of the evidence is limited in a way worth stating. Three of the sources cited here are pages from Library and Archives Canada [3], three are from intellectdiscover.com [13][15][16], and four are DOI-hosted [1][4][10][12]. The central claims about what the McLuhans said rest largely on a single secondary source, Tyler [8], because it is the one source that quotes the book at length with page numbers. If Tyler misreports the wine passage or the checkability sentence, this report repeats the error.

Coverage was thin on two fronts. First, no systematic review or bibliometric study of tetrad applications was found, so the claim that applications are extensive rests on the range of examples encountered rather than on a count. Second, the empirical literature on media displacement is cited here only through Tyler's 2008 summary [8]; the underlying studies — the cross-European project, the Kaiser Family Foundation reports, Yee's Daedalus data — were not read directly, and the numbers in section 6 are as he reports them.

sentences.sentence: Several provinces also set a lower student or subminimum rate that applies to some young workers, so an increase in the general rate does not raise the legal floor for every young worker [4].
Ontario's student rate, for example, applies to students under 18 who work 28 hours a week or less in the school year, or during school breaks and summer holidays [4].
Ontario's general rate went from $11.60 on 1 October 2017 to $14.00 on 1 January 2018 — in a single step, and then stayed at $14.00 until October 2020 [15].
Alberta's went from $12.20 in October 2016 to $13.60 in October 2017 and $15.00 in October 2018, then froze [15].
British Columbia's rose from $11.35 in September 2017 to $13.85 in June 2019 [15].
Saskatchewan's rose from $10.96 in October 2017 to $11.32 in October 2019, an increase of 3.3% over two years [15].

The standard instrument is Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey, Table 14-10-0287, which publishes monthly seasonally adjusted employment, unemployment and participation by age group back to 1976 [8].
The Fraser Institute's survey of fourteen Canadian studies reports elasticities of -0.3 to -0.6 for broad youth groups and -0.45 to -2.0 for directly affected workers [14].
The best-known Canadian provincial panel study reports that a 10% increase is associated with a 1% to 4% reduction in teen employment rates [2].

The best-known Canadian provincial panel study, covering 1981 to 2011, reports that "Ordinary least squares and instrumental variables (IV) estimates imply a 10% increase in minimum wage is associated with a 1%–4% reduction to employment rates for both male and female teens" [2].

Howe Institute commentary by Hugh Marchand, published in 2017, summarised the Canadian literature and concluded that "These estimates implythat a 10 percent increase in the minimum wagewould lead to a 1.7 to 7.5 percent reduction inthe affected employment in Canada" [6].

That range is built from Swidinsky (1980), Baker, Benjamin and Staker (1999), Yuen (2003), Campolieti, Gunderson and Riddell (2006), Sen, Van de Waal and Rybczynski (2011) and Brochu and Green (2013) [6].

The Fraser Institute, reviewing fourteen Canadian studies, split them into two groups: studies of broad youth groups found elasticities of -0.3 to -0.6, and studies of directly affected workers found -0.45 to -2.0 [14].

On those numbers a 20% increase in the wage floor implies youth employment losses of 6% to 12% in the first group, and 9% to 40% among directly affected workers in the second [14]. **The provincial panel evidence.** The best-known Canadian panel study, by Anindya Sen and Krystle Rybczynski in *Contemporary Economic Policy*, used 185 minimum wage amendments across the provinces from 1981 to 2011 [2].

Its abstract states that "Ordinary least squares and instrumental variables (IV) estimates imply a 10% increase in minimum wage is associated with a 1%–4% reduction to employment rates for both male and female teens" [2].

Its headline result: "While the net impact on labour income would be positive, employment would fall by 60,000—a number that lies in the lower part of a range obtained from an accounting exercise (30,000 to 140,000)" [16].

For young workers specifically, applying the sex- and education-controlled elasticities to the 15-to-19 and 20-to-24 age groups implied a reduction of "about 75,000 jobs relative to otherwise by 2019, or about 0.4 per cent of 2016 levels" [16].

The Bank's note also states the prior plainly: "Although empirical evidence is mixed on the magnitude of minimum wage effects,most studies for Canada find that the reduction in employment is statistically significant, especially for younger workers" [16].

It is the central bank's own estimate, made before the fact, that the post-2017 increases would cost young Canadians tens of thousands of jobs. **Alberta, the flagship episode.** Alberta raised its general minimum wage from $12.20 in October 2016 to $13.60 in October 2017 and $15.00 in October 2018, then froze it [15].

Marchand's 2017 commentary tracked the first two steps: "From April 2015 to April 2017, the number ofemployed individuals aged 15-24 in Alberta hasdropped from 326,300 to 298,600, meaning that27,700 of these individuals have already lost theirjobs" [6].
From September 2018 to April 2019, youth part-time employment dropped by 6 percent while Albertans aged 25 and over experienced a less than one percent decline" [10].

Read as an inference rather than a measurement, a 6% fall concentrated on the group whose wage floor rose most, against under 1% for the group whose floor did not, is the kind of comparison the thesis needs [10]. **Ontario, the largest single shock.** Ontario's general rate went from $11.60 on 1 October 2017 to $14.00 on 1 January 2018, in a single step [15].

On the eve of that increase the Fraser Institute published the prediction the case-for can be scored against: "In fact, Canadian research finds that for every 10 per cent increase in the minimum wage, youth employment drops by three to six per cent" [9].

Applied to a step of that size, the same rule of thumb implies 6% to 12% fewer youth jobs in the province that employs the largest number of young Canadians, a calculation from [9] and [15]. **Why the case-for expects the effect to show up in youth.** Exposure is the reason.
In 2013, half of all employees aged 15 to 19 were paid at the minimum wage, against 13% of those aged 20 to 24, and 61% of all minimum wage employees were aged 15 to 24 [1].
A policy that raises the floor therefore touches a much larger share of teenagers than of any other group, and the aggregate data are most likely to detect an effect there [1].

The mechanism also matters for where to look: the effect should appear as reduced hiring rather than layoffs, because firms cut the number of low-wage positions they open rather than dismissing people they already have [1]. **The strongest version of the case.** Taken together, the argument is that Canada's own elasticity estimates, derived from 185 provincial amendments and pooled in two independent reviews, imply youth employment losses of several per cent for increases of the size seen after 2017 [2][6][14].
The central bank's pre-implementation estimate put the national job cost in the tens of thousands, concentrated among the young [16].
Alberta shows a 27,700 fall in youth employment during the first two steps and a 6% fall in youth part-time work after the last one, against under 1% for adults [6][10].
Ontario delivered a 20% increase in a single quarter against a published prediction of a 6% to 12% youth employment loss [9][15].

Marchand's 27,700 figure is a raw before-and-after comparison in a province that was simultaneously absorbing an oil price collapse and a new carbon tax, and he acknowledged the problem: "The true impacts of these minimum wage increasesin Alberta can only be identified with propermeasurement well after the changes take place, sothat outcomes can be compared before, during,and after the policy" [6].

The case against has three parts: the aggregate data do not show the youth job losses the thesis predicts, the timing of the youth deterioration is wrong for a minimum-wage explanation, and the best-identified modern research finds the disemployment mechanism absent even where the wage floor rose much further than in Canada. **Statistics Canada's own reading of the evidence is that aggregate effects are small.** Its analytical review of the minimum wage literature states that "In Canada, the effects of an increase in the minimum wage on total employment would typically be small or non-existent" [1].
The same review then narrows the claim: an increase "would seem to be associated with a decrease in employment among teenagers" [1].
The thesis as stated covers "young workers", a group that includes 20-to-24-year-olds, whose exposure to the floor is roughly a quarter of teenagers' [1].
For older workers, the reduction in layoffs largely offsets the reduction in hirings, with a nil or insignificant effect on employment" [1].

Second, the same policy that reduces teenage hiring also reduces teenage layoffs, so the net employment change is the difference between two movements in opposite directions, and is correspondingly harder to detect [1]. **The pooled Canadian estimate is modest.** Matthew Campolieti's meta-analysis in *Canadian Public Policy* (2020) tested the Canadian literature for publication bias and, for teenagers, found none: "For teenagers, the demographic group with the largest share of minimum wage workers and thus providing the findings of most interest to policy-makers and legislators, I find no evidence of a publication bias" [7].

The meta-analysis pools studies that almost all end before 2017, so it says what the pre-2017 evidence supports, not what happened afterwards [7]. **The timing does not fit.** The largest post-2017 provincial increases took effect between October 2017 and June 2019.

Instead, the national youth employment rate "had trended down from a high of 59.6% in March 2023 to 54.0% in August 2024, a rate not previously seen since February 1999 (excluding 2020 and 2021)" [11].

A policy that was largely finished by 2019 cannot explain a deterioration that began in 2023. **The 2024-25 deterioration has a competing explanation, and it is a supply one.** The fall is concentrated among students: "In September 2025, the unemployment rate among youth attending school was 17.1%, up 3.1 percentage points from the same month in 2024", while the rate for youth not in school was virtually unchanged at 11.9% [11].

Summer 2025 was the worst student job market since the financial crisis: "On average over the months of May to August 2025, the unemployment rate for returning students—those who attended school full time in the spring and intended to return to school full time in the fall—stood at 17.9%, the highest rate since the summer of 2009" [11].

Statistics Canada notes that "The target population includes temporary residents—that is, those with a valid work or study permit, their families, and refugee claimants—as well as permanent residents (landed immigrants) and the Canadian-born" [11].

The authors report: "We find that minimum wage increases do not result in an abnormal concentration of Job Leavers below the new minimum wage, which is inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model" [13].

Our findings are consistent with a model where entry wages are set according to a job ladder, and where firms anchor their internal wage structure on the minimum wage due to fairness or internal incentives issues" [13].
It raises pay without destroying the rungs. **The Alberta episode, read against the thesis.** Alberta's youth employment fell by 27,700 between April 2015 and April 2017 [6].

The author of the 27,700 figure accepted that the causal question was still open [6]. **The strongest version of the case against.** Canada's statistical agency, reviewing the literature, finds aggregate employment effects "small or non-existent" and locates the only real effect in teenagers [1].
The meta-analysis that tests the Canadian literature for publication bias finds none for teenagers, so the modest published estimates stand as they are [7].

The youth labour market was strong through 2022 and only turned in 2023, years after the increases, and the turn is concentrated among students in a period of rapid growth in the youth labour force [11].
The one recent Canadian study that tests the mechanism directly, using the shape of the wage distribution, finds no sign of the job destruction the neoclassical model predicts [13].

It turns on four measurement choices, and on one comparison that nobody has yet published for the post-2017 Canadian increases. **First, the measure: stock or flow, rate or level.** Statistics Canada's review is explicit that "These effects do not necessarily take the form of layoffs, but may instead take the form of reduced hiring, which diminishes the job prospects of teenagers" [1].

The Bank of Canada's estimates suggest this is not a technicality: a 10% rise in the minimum wage relative to average wages is estimated to cut participation by 2.6% for 15-to-19-year-olds and 1.5% for 20-to-24-year-olds, almost as much as it cuts their employment rates [16].

That is a change in the numerator of the employment rate without a corresponding number of jobs disappearing. **Second, the group.** The same Bank of Canada table gives elasticities of -0.33 for ages 15 to 19 and -0.22 for ages 20 to 24, both significant, and -0.07 for all workers aged 15 and over, which is not [16].

Any test of it must state whether it means teenagers or all 15-to-24-year-olds, because the two groups differ by a factor of four in exposure to the floor, as the 2013 shares in section 2 show [1]. **Third, the wage measure used to build the "bite" ratio.** The effect of a minimum wage depends on its level relative to average earnings, not on its dollar value, because that ratio determines how many workers are actually affected [1].

The higher this ratio—that is, the closer the minimum wage to average hourly earnings (all things being equal)—the more workers are affected by minimum wage legislation and the greater the effects on employment" [1].
Statistics Canada also reports Fortin's finding that "when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant" [1].
With SEPH wages over 1995 to 2016 the 15-to-19 elasticity was -0.40 and significant; with LFS wages over the same period it was -0.06 and insignificant [16].
The 1995-to-2008 estimates show the same divergence [16].

The consequence is that the national job-loss estimate from the same legislated increases is either "136,000 jobs by 2019 using the SEPH wage measure and only 30,000 jobs using the LFS wage measure" [16].

The direction of the effect survives; the size does not. **Fourth, the international benchmark for where effects begin.** The most-cited review of the international evidence, by Arindrajit Dube for the UK government, concludes that "Across US states, the best evidence suggests that the employment effects are small up to around 59% of the median wage" [3].
Exactly how far one can push the minimum wage before job losses start becoming pronounced is an empirical question" [3].

The best-identified US study, by Cengiz, Dube, Lindner and Zipperer, examined 138 state minimum wage changes between 1979 and 2016 and found that "the overall number of low-wage jobs remained essentially unchanged over the five years following the increase" [5].

They also report "there is no relationship between the employment estimate and the Kaitz index up to around 59%, confirming that the minimum wage changes in the United States that we study have yet to reach a level above which significant disemployment effects emerge" [5].

The same authors show that specifications finding large aggregate losses are driven by implausible job losses far above the minimum wage: "the specifications that indicate a large negative effect on aggregate employment tend to be driven by an unrealistically large drop in the number of jobs at the upper tail of the wage distribution, which is unlikely to be a causal effect of the minimum wage" [5].

Where they do find losses, they are in tradeable goods, with an own-wage elasticity around -1.4 in manufacturing, and near zero in the non-tradeable sectors where young Canadians actually work [5]. **The crux, stated.** The decisive question is whether the post-2017 Canadian increases pushed provincial minimum wages above the ratio at which effects become detectable, and whether, measured against the right wage series and on the right margin, teenage employment in the provinces with the largest increases fell relative to provinces with small ones.

The international literature locates the onset of detectable effects at a minimum wage of roughly 59% of the median [3], and Fortin locates the onset for Canadian teenagers at close to half of average hourly earnings [1].
Ontario's 2018 step was large in dollar terms [15].
The disemployment finding is real in the Canadian literature for teenagers and it operates through hiring [1].

And the size of that finding is unstable: a factor-of-four swing from the choice of wage deflator, a null for all workers aged 15 and over, and a participation response nearly as large as the employment response [16].

The obstacles are that the increases cluster in 2018 and that 2020 brings a shock large enough to swamp them, which is why the usable post-treatment window is short. **A pooled wage-bin analysis would settle the measurement question.** The Cengiz et al. method counts jobs in narrow wage bands around the new minimum before and after each increase [5].
The Cengiz result for the United States is that the jobs shift rather than disappear [5].
Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend have done something adjacent for Canada, using job leavers and stayers rather than wage bins, and found no bunching below the new minimum [13].
Without knowing whether Ontario in 2018 sat at 45% or 55% of average hourly earnings, neither international benchmark can be applied to it [3][1].

The Bank of Canada's own LFS-wage specification, which gives -0.06 and insignificance for teenagers [16], is close to this result already; what it lacks is post-2017 data. **Evidence that would overturn the case against, specifically.** A finding that Canadian provinces crossed well above the threshold at which the international literature locates the onset of job losses, and still showed no teenage losses, would do it [3].

A demonstration that the 2023-25 youth deterioration was concentrated in provinces with high minimum wages, rather than among students across the country, would also do it; the published data so far point the other way, with the fall concentrated among students in school [11]. **What has been looked at, and what has not.** The pre-2017 literature is thoroughly mined: 185 provincial amendments [2], a meta-analysis testing for publication bias [7], turnover decompositions [13], and the central bank's own simulation [16].

Howe analyses of Alberta [10], the Fraser Institute's pre-increase predictions [9][14], and a 2026 SSRN working paper using machine learning on Canadian youth employment [4], which was not readable in full for this report.

The Dube review makes the point about Seattle: single case studies are where quirks dominate, and the Seattle dispute turned on whether measured job losses were really wage growth pushing workers into higher wage bins [3].
Quirks—like unusually high wage growth in Seattle—are much more likely to affect individual cases, making it hard to convincingly separate out signal from noise" [3].

A precise thesis must therefore commit to a magnitude and population ("teens", i.e. 15-19, not all youth 15-24), not just a sign.

This is the single most useful benchmark for the section: the Canadian thesis becomes falsifiable once Canadian provincial minimums are measured against median wages — if post-2017 Canadian rates stayed near or below this range, finding youth job losses would be an outlier result requiring strong identification; if they pushed well above it, the thesis gains prior plausibility.

This defines what would overturn the anti-thesis: a demonstration that Canadian post-2017 increases were large enough and concentrated enough (high bite, rapid, multi-province) to cross into the range where disemployment is expected.
