report.body:
## TL;DR

**Verdict: Unsettled.** It is about as likely as not that the post-2017 provincial increases reduced youth employment in the aggregate, and the question turns on a measurement nobody has published. Canadian studies do find negative teenage elasticities [1][2][16], but the same dataset yields a null for all workers aged 15 and over [16], the national job-loss estimate swings from 30,000 to 136,000 on the choice of wage deflator [16], the youth labour market only turned in 2023, and the turn is concentrated among students [11]. The crux is whether the increases pushed provincial minimum wages above the ratio at which effects become detectable, and where that ratio actually stood is unknown.

## Key Findings

- The published Canadian literature mostly finds a negative effect on teenagers: a 10% increase is associated with a 1% to 4% reduction in teen employment rates in the main provincial panel study [2], and the Fraser Institute's survey of fourteen studies reports elasticities of -0.3 to -0.6 for broad youth groups [14].
- The Bank of Canada's pre-implementation estimate was that the scheduled increases would cost about 60,000 jobs nationally by 2019, with a range of 30,000 to 140,000, and about 75,000 jobs among 15-to-24-year-olds [16].
- The same Bank of Canada note shows the estimate is unstable: using LFS wages rather than SEPH wages, the national figure falls from 136,000 to 30,000 jobs, and the teenage elasticity from -0.40 to -0.06 and insignificant [16].
- Statistics Canada's own review states that aggregate employment effects in Canada are "small or non-existent", with the effect concentrated on teenagers and operating through reduced hiring rather than layoffs [1].
- Youth employment in Canada did not deteriorate when the increases took effect. The youth employment rate fell from 59.6% in March 2023 to 54.0% in August 2024, four to six years later [11].
- The 2024-25 deterioration is concentrated among students: youth unemployment in school rose 3.1 points to 17.1% while the rate for youth not in school was virtually unchanged at 11.9%, and summer 2025 was the worst student job market since 2009 [11].
- The best-identified recent Canadian study finds no abnormal bunching of job leavers below the new minimum wage, which is inconsistent with the job-destruction mechanism, and instead finds the wage ladder shifted up [13].
- The international benchmark is that US employment effects are small up to about 59% of the median wage, above which the evidence thins [3][5]; whether Canadian provinces crossed that line has not been established.
- Alberta, the flagship case for the thesis, raised its rate from $12.20 to $15.00 between October 2016 and October 2018 during an oil-price collapse, and the author of the 27,700 youth job-loss figure conceded that causal identification had to wait [6][15].

## Details

### 1. The thesis, stated precisely: what "reduced employment among young workers" claims, what it leaves out, and what would falsify it

The claim to be tested is this: the increases in provincial general minimum wage rates that Canada's provinces legislated and implemented from 2017 onward caused a reduction in the number of employed young workers (aged 15 to 24, and especially teenagers aged 15 to 19) in the provinces where those increases were largest, relative to what would have happened without them.

Three parts of that sentence need pinning down, because the claim as stated can be read in ways that change the answer.

**Which rate rose.** Minimum wages are set by each province, not federally, so "raising provincial minimum wages" describes at least ten separate policy experiments with different sizes, timings and phase-ins. Several provinces also set a lower student or subminimum rate that applies to some young workers, so an increase in the general rate does not raise the legal floor for every young worker [4]. Ontario's student rate, for example, applies to students under 18 who work 28 hours a week or less in the school year, or during school breaks and summer holidays [4]. A claim about "young workers" therefore has to say whether it means teenagers subject to the general adult rate, all 15-to-24-year-olds, or the narrower group of part-time under-18 students whose statutory floor may not have moved.

**Which period.** "Since 2017" covers unusually large and unusually clustered increases. Ontario's general rate went from $11.60 on 1 October 2017 to $14.00 on 1 January 2018 — in a single step, and then stayed at $14.00 until October 2020 [15]. Alberta's went from $12.20 in October 2016 to $13.60 in October 2017 and $15.00 in October 2018, then froze [15]. British Columbia's rose from $11.35 in September 2017 to $13.85 in June 2019 [15]. Saskatchewan's rose from $10.96 in October 2017 to $11.32 in October 2019, an increase of 3.3% over two years [15]. That spread is what makes the question answerable: the comparison across provinces with very different increases is the identification.

**Which measure of employment.** "Reduced employment" can mean a fall in the number of young people employed, in the youth employment rate, in hours worked, or in the probability that a minimum-wage earner keeps a job. These can move in different directions. The standard instrument is Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey, Table 14-10-0287, which publishes monthly seasonally adjusted employment, unemployment and participation by age group back to 1976 [8]. An employment rate can fall because jobs fell, or because the youth population and school enrolment rose while the number of jobs stayed flat; an employment level can fall for the same reason. The claim is falsifiable only once the series is specified.

**What magnitude would count.** The claim is about a sign, but the published Canadian ranges mostly put the sign at negative, and disagree about size. The Fraser Institute's survey of fourteen Canadian studies reports elasticities of -0.3 to -0.6 for broad youth groups and -0.45 to -2.0 for directly affected workers [14]. The best-known Canadian provincial panel study reports that a 10% increase is associated with a 1% to 4% reduction in teen employment rates [2]. The best-known Canadian provincial panel study, covering 1981 to 2011, reports that "Ordinary least squares and instrumental variables (IV) estimates imply a 10% increase in minimum wage is associated with a 1%–4% reduction to employment rates for both male and female teens" [2]. So a claim that the sign is negative is close to the mainstream prior; what is genuinely contestable is whether increases of the size seen since 2017 actually produced detectable losses in the aggregate data, and whether the observed weakness in youth employment in that period is attributable to the wage floor rather than to the other things happening at the same time.

**How the claim could be shown wrong.** Three ways. First, if youth employment in provinces with large increases did not fall relative to comparable provinces with small ones, after allowing for province-specific trends. Second, if the falls that did occur are fully accounted for by identifiable shocks that hit the same provinces at the same time — in Canada after 2017, above all the collapse in oil prices and investment in Alberta and Saskatchewan, and the COVID-19 shutdowns of 2020, which fell hardest on the sectors that employ young workers. Third, if the estimated losses exist only for directly affected minimum-wage workers and are offset by higher earnings, more hours, or reallocation into better jobs, so that aggregate youth employment is unchanged.

**The reading tested here.** The report tests the aggregate reading — that the post-2017 provincial increases reduced youth employment in the data — because that is the claim a reader would take from the sentence. The narrower reading, that the policy reduced employment among the specific workers whose wage floor rose, is treated as a distinct and better-supported claim in its own right, and it is where most of the credible evidence actually sits.

What the claim does not assert, and should not be read as asserting, is that the increases reduced total employment in the economy, or that they made young workers worse off overall. A minimum wage that costs some young people a job while raising the pay of those who keep one can leave the group's total earnings higher; the thesis is about employment, and only about employment.

### 2. The strongest case for: the studies and episodes that find youth job losses from Canadian minimum wage rises since 2017

The case for the thesis does not rest on one study. It rests on a Canadian elasticity literature that is unusually consistent in sign, on two large natural experiments that were predicted in advance, and on the arithmetic of how large the post-2017 increases were relative to anything Canada had done before.

**The Canadian estimates are larger than the American ones.** A C.D. Howe Institute commentary by Hugh Marchand, published in 2017, summarised the Canadian literature and concluded that "These estimates implythat a 10 percent increase in the minimum wagewould lead to a 1.7 to 7.5 percent reduction inthe affected employment in Canada" [6]. That range is built from Swidinsky (1980), Baker, Benjamin and Staker (1999), Yuen (2003), Campolieti, Gunderson and Riddell (2006), Sen, Van de Waal and Rybczynski (2011) and Brochu and Green (2013) [6]. The Fraser Institute, reviewing fourteen Canadian studies, split them into two groups: studies of broad youth groups found elasticities of -0.3 to -0.6, and studies of directly affected workers found -0.45 to -2.0 [14]. On those numbers a 20% increase in the wage floor implies youth employment losses of 6% to 12% in the first group, and 9% to 40% among directly affected workers in the second [14].

**The provincial panel evidence.** The best-known Canadian panel study, by Anindya Sen and Krystle Rybczynski in *Contemporary Economic Policy*, used 185 minimum wage amendments across the provinces from 1981 to 2011 [2]. Its abstract states that "Ordinary least squares and instrumental variables (IV) estimates imply a 10% increase in minimum wage is associated with a 1%–4% reduction to employment rates for both male and female teens" [2]. That is a two-to-four-times larger effect than the null that the case against needs, and it is estimated on Canadian data with province and year fixed effects and province-specific trends.

**The Bank of Canada put a number on the scheduled increases.** In December 2017, before most of the increases took effect, the Bank published a staff analytical note that applied updated versions of Pierre Fortin's provincial elasticities to the increases then legislated in Ontario, Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia. Its headline result: "While the net impact on labour income would be positive, employment would fall by 60,000—a number that lies in the lower part of a range obtained from an accounting exercise (30,000 to 140,000)" [16]. For young workers specifically, applying the sex- and education-controlled elasticities to the 15-to-19 and 20-to-24 age groups implied a reduction of "about 75,000 jobs relative to otherwise by 2019, or about 0.4 per cent of 2016 levels" [16]. The Bank's note also states the prior plainly: "Although empirical evidence is mixed on the magnitude of minimum wage effects,most studies for Canada find that the reduction in employment is statistically significant, especially for younger workers" [16]. This is not an advocacy document. It is the central bank's own estimate, made before the fact, that the post-2017 increases would cost young Canadians tens of thousands of jobs.

**Alberta, the flagship episode.** Alberta raised its general minimum wage from $12.20 in October 2016 to $13.60 in October 2017 and $15.00 in October 2018, then froze it [15]. Marchand's 2017 commentary tracked the first two steps: "From April 2015 to April 2017, the number ofemployed individuals aged 15-24 in Alberta hasdropped from 326,300 to 298,600, meaning that27,700 of these individuals have already lost theirjobs" [6]. That fall came before the largest single step and exceeded Marchand's own predicted loss for the age group.

The second Alberta test came after the final step. Parisa Mahboubi of the C.D. Howe Institute compared youth part-time employment in the months after the October 2018 increase with the same months a year earlier, when the pattern ran the other way. Her finding: "Overall, Alberta's minimum wage increase to $15 per hour on October 1, 2018 had a larger negative impact on part-time employment of youth relative to other minimum wage workers. From September 2018 to April 2019, youth part-time employment dropped by 6 percent while Albertans aged 25 and over experienced a less than one percent decline" [10]. Read as an inference rather than a measurement, a 6% fall concentrated on the group whose wage floor rose most, against under 1% for the group whose floor did not, is the kind of comparison the thesis needs [10].

**Ontario, the largest single shock.** Ontario's general rate went from $11.60 on 1 October 2017 to $14.00 on 1 January 2018, in a single step [15]. On the eve of that increase the Fraser Institute published the prediction the case-for can be scored against: "In fact, Canadian research finds that for every 10 per cent increase in the minimum wage, youth employment drops by three to six per cent" [9]. Applied to a step of that size, the same rule of thumb implies 6% to 12% fewer youth jobs in the province that employs the largest number of young Canadians, a calculation from [9] and [15].

**Why the case-for expects the effect to show up in youth.** Exposure is the reason. In 2013, half of all employees aged 15 to 19 were paid at the minimum wage, against 13% of those aged 20 to 24, and 61% of all minimum wage employees were aged 15 to 24 [1]. A policy that raises the floor therefore touches a much larger share of teenagers than of any other group, and the aggregate data are most likely to detect an effect there [1]. The mechanism also matters for where to look: the effect should appear as reduced hiring rather than layoffs, because firms cut the number of low-wage positions they open rather than dismissing people they already have [1].

**The strongest version of the case.** Taken together, the argument is that Canada's own elasticity estimates, derived from 185 provincial amendments and pooled in two independent reviews, imply youth employment losses of several per cent for increases of the size seen after 2017 [2][6][14]. The central bank's pre-implementation estimate put the national job cost in the tens of thousands, concentrated among the young [16]. Alberta shows a 27,700 fall in youth employment during the first two steps and a 6% fall in youth part-time work after the last one, against under 1% for adults [6][10]. Ontario delivered a 20% increase in a single quarter against a published prediction of a 6% to 12% youth employment loss [9][15]. On this reading the thesis is not a prediction about what might happen; it is a description of what the Canadian literature said would happen, followed by episodes consistent with it.

**The concession inside the case-for.** The case is weaker than it looks in one respect, and its own authors say so. Marchand's 27,700 figure is a raw before-and-after comparison in a province that was simultaneously absorbing an oil price collapse and a new carbon tax, and he acknowledged the problem: "The true impacts of these minimum wage increasesin Alberta can only be identified with propermeasurement well after the changes take place, sothat outcomes can be compared before, during,and after the policy" [6]. The Alberta numbers are therefore consistent with the thesis without yet being evidence for it. What the case-for really has is a well-specified prior, a central bank simulation built on that prior, and two episodes that have not been separated from the shocks that hit them.

### 3. The strongest case against: what the same and other evidence shows, and the alternative explanations for weak youth employment after 2017

The case against has three parts: the aggregate data do not show the youth job losses the thesis predicts, the timing of the youth deterioration is wrong for a minimum-wage explanation, and the best-identified modern research finds the disemployment mechanism absent even where the wage floor rose much further than in Canada.

**Statistics Canada's own reading of the evidence is that aggregate effects are small.** Its analytical review of the minimum wage literature states that "In Canada, the effects of an increase in the minimum wage on total employment would typically be small or non-existent" [1]. The same review then narrows the claim: an increase "would seem to be associated with a decrease in employment among teenagers" [1]. That sentence is the case against in miniature. The thesis as stated covers "young workers", a group that includes 20-to-24-year-olds, whose exposure to the floor is roughly a quarter of teenagers' [1]. For that broader group the expected effect is small, and for the workforce as a whole it is nil.

**The effect is concentrated in a specific margin, and that matters for what a null result means.** Statistics Canada's summary of Brochu and Green (2012) is that "when the minimum wage is high, labour market transitions (hirings and layoffs) tend to decrease. For teenagers, the reductions in hirings largely exceed the number of layoffs, which explains why there is a significant and negative effect on employment in this age group. For older workers, the reduction in layoffs largely offsets the reduction in hirings, with a nil or insignificant effect on employment" [1]. The mechanism is fewer job openings, not dismissals. That has two consequences the case against can use. First, an effect that runs through hiring is slow to show up in a stock measure like the employment rate, and it should appear most plainly in flows. Second, the same policy that reduces teenage hiring also reduces teenage layoffs, so the net employment change is the difference between two movements in opposite directions, and is correspondingly harder to detect [1].

**The pooled Canadian estimate is modest.** Matthew Campolieti's meta-analysis in *Canadian Public Policy* (2020) tested the Canadian literature for publication bias and, for teenagers, found none: "For teenagers, the demographic group with the largest share of minimum wage workers and thus providing the findings of most interest to policy-makers and legislators, I find no evidence of a publication bias" [7]. That is a point in favour of the literature's credibility rather than against it. It also means the published teenage estimates are not inflated by selective reporting, and those estimates are mostly modest. The meta-analysis pools studies that almost all end before 2017, so it says what the pre-2017 evidence supports, not what happened afterwards [7].

**The timing does not fit.** The largest post-2017 provincial increases took effect between October 2017 and June 2019. If they had reduced youth employment, the damage should appear in 2018 and 2019. Instead, the national youth employment rate "had trended down from a high of 59.6% in March 2023 to 54.0% in August 2024, a rate not previously seen since February 1999 (excluding 2020 and 2021)" [11]. The collapse came four to six years after the wage-floor increases and during a period in which most provinces had frozen or indexed their minimum wages. A policy that was largely finished by 2019 cannot explain a deterioration that began in 2023.

**The 2024-25 deterioration has a competing explanation, and it is a supply one.** The fall is concentrated among students: "In September 2025, the unemployment rate among youth attending school was 17.1%, up 3.1 percentage points from the same month in 2024", while the rate for youth not in school was virtually unchanged at 11.9% [11]. Summer 2025 was the worst student job market since the financial crisis: "On average over the months of May to August 2025, the unemployment rate for returning students—those who attended school full time in the spring and intended to return to school full time in the fall—stood at 17.9%, the highest rate since the summer of 2009" [11]. No province made a matching minimum wage change in 2025. What did change was the size of the youth labour force. Statistics Canada notes that "The target population includes temporary residents—that is, those with a valid work or study permit, their families, and refugee claimants—as well as permanent residents (landed immigrants) and the Canadian-born" [11]. Rapid growth in the number of young people looking for work, at a time when hiring was slowing, produces exactly the pattern observed, and it does so without any contribution from the wage floor.

**The best-identified Canadian study finds the disemployment mechanism missing.** David Brochu, David Green, Thomas Lemieux and James Townsend's 2025 NBER working paper, "The Minimum Wage, Turnover, and the Shape of the Wage Distribution", tests the neoclassical prediction directly on Canadian data. If a higher minimum wage destroyed jobs, workers who would have been hired just below the new floor should bunch just below it instead. The authors report: "We find that minimum wage increases do not result in an abnormal concentration of Job Leavers below the new minimum wage, which is inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model" [13]. They offer an alternative account of what minimum wages do: "We also find that, for Job Stayers, the spike and spillover effects of the minimum wage are simply shifted right to the new minimum wage. Our findings are consistent with a model where entry wages are set according to a job ladder, and where firms anchor their internal wage structure on the minimum wage due to fairness or internal incentives issues" [13]. On this account a minimum wage increase moves the whole entry ladder up. It raises pay without destroying the rungs.

**The Alberta episode, read against the thesis.** Alberta's youth employment fell by 27,700 between April 2015 and April 2017 [6]. In those same two years the price of oil collapsed, and Alberta's economy contracted more than any other province's. The counterfactual for a young Albertan in 2016 was not the same labour market with a lower minimum wage, but a labour market in which investment in the oil sands had stopped. Attributing the whole fall to the wage floor requires showing that youth employment in Alberta would have held up in a severe regional recession, which no study has shown. The author of the 27,700 figure accepted that the causal question was still open [6].

**The strongest version of the case against.** Canada's statistical agency, reviewing the literature, finds aggregate employment effects "small or non-existent" and locates the only real effect in teenagers [1]. The meta-analysis that tests the Canadian literature for publication bias finds none for teenagers, so the modest published estimates stand as they are [7]. The youth labour market was strong through 2022 and only turned in 2023, years after the increases, and the turn is concentrated among students in a period of rapid growth in the youth labour force [11]. The one recent Canadian study that tests the mechanism directly, using the shape of the wage distribution, finds no sign of the job destruction the neoclassical model predicts [13]. On this reading, the thesis mistakes a plausible theoretical prior for a measured fact, and the measured fact points the other way.

### 4. The crux: the measure, margin and comparison that decide it, and what the best-identified studies show so far

The disagreement does not turn on whether a price floor can cost jobs. Both sides concede it can. It turns on four measurement choices, and on one comparison that nobody has yet published for the post-2017 Canadian increases.

**First, the measure: stock or flow, rate or level.** Statistics Canada's review is explicit that "These effects do not necessarily take the form of layoffs, but may instead take the form of reduced hiring, which diminishes the job prospects of teenagers" [1]. An effect that operates through hiring shows up in separations and hiring rates, not in the employment stock for months or years. It also shows up differently in an employment rate than in an employment level. The employment rate can fall while the number of employed young people is unchanged, if the youth population rises. The Bank of Canada's estimates suggest this is not a technicality: a 10% rise in the minimum wage relative to average wages is estimated to cut participation by 2.6% for 15-to-19-year-olds and 1.5% for 20-to-24-year-olds, almost as much as it cuts their employment rates [16]. A large share of what a naive reading calls "lost jobs" is young people leaving the labour force, usually for school. That is a change in the numerator of the employment rate without a corresponding number of jobs disappearing.

**Second, the group.** The same Bank of Canada table gives elasticities of -0.33 for ages 15 to 19 and -0.22 for ages 20 to 24, both significant, and -0.07 for all workers aged 15 and over, which is not [16]. One dataset, one specification family, and the answer runs from a clear negative to a null depending on which age band is used. The thesis says "young workers", which spans both. Any test of it must state whether it means teenagers or all 15-to-24-year-olds, because the two groups differ by a factor of four in exposure to the floor, as the 2013 shares in section 2 show [1].

**Third, the wage measure used to build the "bite" ratio.** The effect of a minimum wage depends on its level relative to average earnings, not on its dollar value, because that ratio determines how many workers are actually affected [1]. Statistics Canada states the criterion directly: "The extent of the effect on employment depends on a number of factors,Note 4 including the ratio of the minimum wage to the average hourly earnings (AHE). The higher this ratio—that is, the closer the minimum wage to average hourly earnings (all things being equal)—the more workers are affected by minimum wage legislation and the greater the effects on employment" [1]. Statistics Canada also reports Fortin's finding that "when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant" [1].

Here the Canadian evidence has a serious problem, and it is the sharpest single fact in this report. The Bank of Canada ran its own elasticities two ways, using SEPH wages and using LFS wages. With SEPH wages over 1995 to 2016 the 15-to-19 elasticity was -0.40 and significant; with LFS wages over the same period it was -0.06 and insignificant [16]. The 1995-to-2008 estimates show the same divergence [16]. The consequence is that the national job-loss estimate from the same legislated increases is either "136,000 jobs by 2019 using the SEPH wage measure and only 30,000 jobs using the LFS wage measure" [16]. A finding that moves by a factor of four or more depending on which wage series is used to deflate the minimum wage is not a settled finding. The direction of the effect survives; the size does not.

**Fourth, the international benchmark for where effects begin.** The most-cited review of the international evidence, by Arindrajit Dube for the UK government, concludes that "Across US states, the best evidence suggests that the employment effects are small up to around 59% of the median wage" [3]. It also states the limit of that finding: "Of course, eventually a higher minimum wage will lower employment. Exactly how far one can push the minimum wage before job losses start becoming pronounced is an empirical question" [3]. The best-identified US study, by Cengiz, Dube, Lindner and Zipperer, examined 138 state minimum wage changes between 1979 and 2016 and found that "the overall number of low-wage jobs remained essentially unchanged over the five years following the increase" [5]. Their explanation is that missing jobs just below the new minimum are offset almost exactly by excess jobs just above it. They also report "there is no relationship between the employment estimate and the Kaitz index up to around 59%, confirming that the minimum wage changes in the United States that we study have yet to reach a level above which significant disemployment effects emerge" [5]. The same authors show that specifications finding large aggregate losses are driven by implausible job losses far above the minimum wage: "the specifications that indicate a large negative effect on aggregate employment tend to be driven by an unrealistically large drop in the number of jobs at the upper tail of the wage distribution, which is unlikely to be a causal effect of the minimum wage" [5]. Where they do find losses, they are in tradeable goods, with an own-wage elasticity around -1.4 in manufacturing, and near zero in the non-tradeable sectors where young Canadians actually work [5].

**The crux, stated.** The decisive question is whether the post-2017 Canadian increases pushed provincial minimum wages above the ratio at which effects become detectable, and whether, measured against the right wage series and on the right margin, teenage employment in the provinces with the largest increases fell relative to provinces with small ones. The international literature locates the onset of detectable effects at a minimum wage of roughly 59% of the median [3], and Fortin locates the onset for Canadian teenagers at close to half of average hourly earnings [1]. Ontario's 2018 step was large in dollar terms [15]. No study read for this report establishes where it placed Ontario's ratio against either threshold. That is a gap in the published record rather than a finding about Ontario. That is the missing measurement. Without it, neither side can say whether the increases crossed into the range where the international literature expects job losses, and the disagreement cannot be resolved by citing elasticities estimated at unknown bite.

**What the crux does settle.** Two things. The disemployment finding is real in the Canadian literature for teenagers and it operates through hiring [1]. And the size of that finding is unstable: a factor-of-four swing from the choice of wage deflator, a null for all workers aged 15 and over, and a participation response nearly as large as the employment response [16]. A thesis stated about "employment among young workers" without specifying the group, the measure and the wage series is not yet a testable claim, and the evidence cannot be said to support or refute it until those are fixed.

### 5. What would change the conclusion: the evidence that would overturn it, and whether anyone has looked

What would overturn the conclusion, in either direction, is specific and largely uncollected.

**To overturn the case against, someone would need to publish the post-2017 Canadian test.** No study read for this report estimates the effect of the 2017-2019 provincial increases on youth employment using the variation those increases created. That is the central gap. The design is not exotic: it requires provincial youth employment rates from the Labour Force Survey from 2010 to 2022, the ESDC historical minimum wage series, a wage deflator, and a difference-in-differences or synthetic control specification comparing Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia against Saskatchewan, Manitoba and the Atlantic provinces. The data exist publicly [15]. The obstacles are that the increases cluster in 2018 and that 2020 brings a shock large enough to swamp them, which is why the usable post-treatment window is short.

**A pooled wage-bin analysis would settle the measurement question.** The Cengiz et al. method counts jobs in narrow wage bands around the new minimum before and after each increase [5]. Applied to Canadian provinces, it would show directly whether jobs disappeared below the new floor or merely shifted up. The Cengiz result for the United States is that the jobs shift rather than disappear [5]. Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend have done something adjacent for Canada, using job leavers and stayers rather than wage bins, and found no bunching below the new minimum [13]. A full wage-bin replication on Canadian provincial data would be the strongest single piece of evidence available, and it has not been published.

**The bite ratio for each province and year needs to be computed and published.** This is the cheapest missing measurement and the one that most limits the current debate. Without knowing whether Ontario in 2018 sat at 45% or 55% of average hourly earnings, neither international benchmark can be applied to it [3][1]. Anyone with the LFS wage tables and the ESDC rate series can compute it in an afternoon.

**Evidence that would overturn the case for, specifically.** A well-identified post-2017 Canadian estimate of the teenage own-wage elasticity close to zero, on the hiring margin as well as the stock, would do it. So would a demonstration that youth employment in Ontario and Alberta tracked the provinces with small increases through 2018 and 2019 once regional economic conditions are controlled for. The Bank of Canada's own LFS-wage specification, which gives -0.06 and insignificance for teenagers [16], is close to this result already; what it lacks is post-2017 data.

**Evidence that would overturn the case against, specifically.** A finding that Canadian provinces crossed well above the threshold at which the international literature locates the onset of job losses, and still showed no teenage losses, would do it [3]. A demonstration that the 2023-25 youth deterioration was concentrated in provinces with high minimum wages, rather than among students across the country, would also do it; the published data so far point the other way, with the fall concentrated among students in school [11].

**What has been looked at, and what has not.** The pre-2017 literature is thoroughly mined: 185 provincial amendments [2], a meta-analysis testing for publication bias [7], turnover decompositions [13], and the central bank's own simulation [16]. The post-2017 period is thin. The published work on it that surfaced in this search is advocacy-institute commentary, the C.D. Howe analyses of Alberta [10], the Fraser Institute's pre-increase predictions [9][14], and a 2026 SSRN working paper using machine learning on Canadian youth employment [4], which was not readable in full for this report. No peer-reviewed evaluation of the 2017-2019 increases was found.

**One thing that would not change the conclusion.** More province-level case studies of the Alberta or Ontario type, read as raw before-and-after comparisons, would not settle it. The Dube review makes the point about Seattle: single case studies are where quirks dominate, and the Seattle dispute turned on whether measured job losses were really wage growth pushing workers into higher wage bins [3]. "The exchange over the Seattle evidence also highlights the limits of single case studies like the one from Seattle. Quirks—like unusually high wage growth in Seattle—are much more likely to affect individual cases, making it hard to convincingly separate out signal from noise" [3]. Canada has ten provinces and two decades of variation. The answer, if it exists, is in the pooled data.


## Open questions

**No published evaluation of the 2017-2019 increases exists in the peer-reviewed literature.** The report searched for one and did not find it. Everything specific to the post-2017 period in this record is advocacy-institute commentary [9][10][14], the central bank's pre-implementation simulation [16], and a 2026 SSRN working paper that could not be read in full [4]. The Canadian evidence base for the thesis is therefore almost entirely pre-2017, which is the single largest limitation on any verdict.

**The bite ratio for each province and year has not been computed here.** The international thresholds — roughly 59% of the median wage [3] and Fortin's 50% of average hourly earnings [1] — cannot be applied to the post-2017 increases without knowing where each province stood. That calculation is possible from public data but was not done for this report, and it is the fact the disagreement turns on.

**Whether the effect shows on the hiring margin in the post-2017 data is unknown.** Statistics Canada's summary of Brochu and Green says the teenage effect runs through hiring rather than layoffs [1], and the Bank of Canada's participation elasticities suggest much of any measured "employment" loss is young people leaving the labour force for school [16]. No study read for this report separates those channels for 2017 onward.

**The independence of the sources limits how much weight the case for can carry.** Several of the sources counted for the case for share text: [3], [6], [14] and [16] share long passages word for word, and [6] and [10] are both C.D. Howe Institute publications, as [9] and [14] are both Fraser Institute publications. [1], [8] and [11] are all Statistics Canada. [2] and [7] appear to be copies of the same captured pages. The report treats each institution as one voice when weighing. The apparent breadth of the case for therefore rests on fewer independent estimates than the citation count suggests.

**Coverage of the dissenting Canadian literature is thin.** The report did not locate a peer-reviewed Canadian study arguing for a null or positive youth employment effect from the post-2017 increases, and the strongest available counter-evidence is international [3][5] or about the mechanism rather than the period [13]. If such a study exists, it was missed.

**One flag left standing.** Section 1's statement of what magnitude would count was revised to report the published ranges rather than a single consensus band. The ranges as stated come from [2] and [14] and do not represent a uniform finding across the Canadian literature.

## Beyond this question

The pattern here will repeat wherever a policy is large enough to be interesting and recent enough to be unstudied. The Bank of Canada note is the model of what good practice looks like: it published its estimate and its sensitivity before the policy took effect, which is why the disagreement can now be scored rather than argued [16]. The second lesson is about the wage deflator. A finding that moves by a factor of four when the denominator changes from SEPH to LFS wages [16] is not a fact about the minimum wage; it is a fact about measurement, and it should be reported as such. Anyone evaluating a provincial wage floor should publish the ratio of the minimum to average hourly earnings alongside the elasticity, because without it the estimate cannot be compared to anything.
